using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, projections are matched and grouped through a novel clustering algorithm based on maximum weighted points. Finally, a minimum-cost network is built to determine the 6-DoF object pose that fulfils correspondence constraints across all instances present in the image. Our proposed approach has several advantages over conventional two-stage pipelines. Firstly, heatmaps can be employed as intermediate cues, bypassing the need to extract local features from CNN. Secondly, projection grouping and correspondence are integrated in a hierarchical manner, enabling the utilization of multiple instances per class, which enhances two-stage pipelines. Our proposed approach has been evaluated on three public datasets: LP360, BKP, and ITOD, with results showing significant performance improvements. CT scans can be very difficult for humans and computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Combining images with additional information and restricting the search space to accurately position and boundary tumors is a promising area of research called medical image analysis with prior knowledge. While this approach has been effective in analyzing brain and breast images, its potential for analyzing CT scans of the neck has received little attention. Even less common is the use of prior knowledge that includes spatial and functional information derived from other imaging techniques and physiological data. To explore the potential of this approach for analyzing whole-neck CT scans, an automatic method for marking tumors on CT scans was tested using a range of prior knowledge including boundary maps from tightly related imaging scans, tightly related functional images, and tightly related physiological data. The results showed that incorporating prior knowledge from other imaging techniques and physiological data can significantly improve the accuracy of tumor boundary detection. Furthermore, selecting specific features from these sources, such as the enteral tube, helped to improve performance by reducing noise and external interference. Enteral tubes inserted during scans often complicate boundary detection due to their hard, dense structure that produces high contrast with the surrounding tissue. To test the robustness of the method, enteral tubes were automatically detected and removed from the prior knowledge, which significantly improved boundary detection performance

His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments. 
Our findings show that ReCross successfully expands its task domain with little computational expense, thereby demonstrating its applicability to a wide range of tasks, including but not limited to T0 and FLAN across various domains. 
In addition to this, we also discovered a lesser-known advantage of ReCross - it boosts the model's performance on low-data tasks through efficient knowledge transfer. 
This study's outcomes are backed by rigorous evaluations, including both quantitative metrics and qualitative analysis of generated text. 
The proposed method exhibits an exceptionally compact index, making it scalable to massive datasets, and our results indicate that ReCross surpasses a non-retrieval method by a significant margin, with an average improvement of 12.5% in F0.5 score.

Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's parameters, training data, and activation values. However, recent studies have demonstrated that a simplified model can also be trained to emulate the performance of a complex network using only the model's output, bypassing the need for access to the original network's information. This phenomenon has been termed "knowledge distillation by operating on the output." It has been observed that a heavily compressed model, trained in this way, can achieve comparable performance to a dense model on small neural networks. Furthermore, we find that the effectiveness of output knowledge distillation is positively correlated with the degree of class imbalance in the dataset, and methods that modify the optimization process can enhance the efficacy of output knowledge distillation. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall motion of an object and the motion of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Further enhancements are achieved through adjustment of GMM parameters and feedback encoding, yielding nearly optimal performance in comparison to traditional methods relying on actual channel estimation. Simulation outcomes under various conditions highlight the proposed method's effectiveness in reducing feedback load while improving system performance. 

In this research, we examine the precoder codebook learning problem via Gaussian mixture models, exploring several key aspects. Furthermore, discussion is presented on several practical issues, including precoder codebook learning with multiple models, delay compensation, and 5G NR. One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Our results show that contemporary virtual agents already excel at the three games, consistently achieving near-perfect scores across multiple challenging levels. 
To validate the utility of TextWorldExpress, we created new, complex levels that, in contrast to the original games, require a high level of efficiency to solve, imposing a much greater limit on virtual agents' ability to process information quickly. 
Under these conditions, the improvement in action-per-second speed becomes even more pronounced, leading to a significant shift in the preferred solution strategy from agents, showcasing the significance of addressing this limitation in future research. 
Our research is accompanied by enhanced benchmark guidelines that incorporate the newly developed environments and streamlined challenge frameworks for twenty widely used text-based games. 
We hope that TextWorldExpress sparks widespread adoption of faster game challenges among researchers, facilitating a more rigorous evaluation of virtual agents in complex, real-world scenarios.

This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. Without this feature, the model significantly overestimates the disorders' reach and fails to accurately capture the observed block-level rioting intensity. To address this limitation, we propose a model modification: integrating a feature that more accurately captures the disorders' spatial extension and facilitates representation of the city's layout, without relying on the model's default epidemiological parameters. This revised model, when applied to Santiago's riots, yields results that more closely align with the actual block-level rioting intensity and extent. This project's findings also imply that the disorders' spatial spread was primarily driven by the existing population's willingness to participate, rather than the migration of outsiders. Furthermore, we discovered that the model's effectiveness can vary depending on the chosen layout representation, highlighting the importance of this aspect in modeling the spread of disorders in urban environments. This project's outcomes provide a basis for future work aimed at improving the model's ability to capture the observed distribution of riots in Santiago, as well as other similar episodes

This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier studies, we have bypassed the assumption of constant entropy profiles in our calculations. Instead, we have achieved the desired equilibrium state by solving the balance equations for fluid elements in the superposition of the gravitational field. This has enabled us to determine the full spacetime geometry. We have validated our novel approach by recreating earlier results, including the famous Kepler's problem and Maizel's constant entropy profiles. Additionally, we have obtained two new equilibrium configurations: one with a monopole gravitational field and another with a bipolar field, both featuring inhomogeneous and non-uniform entropy distributions. These findings represent significant milestones in the field of rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. 

The novel approach has been implemented in a specially designed code and made publicly available. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to explain the formation and maintenance of negative temperature states. A simple model incorporating three energy levels and interacting with a reservoir through two-photon processes is utilized to demonstrate the practical application of negative temperature. This model, though straightforward, showcases the appearance of negative temperature in specific energy ranges and highlights the limitations of quantum statistical mechanics when dealing with discrete energy spectra. Moreover, it highlights the marginal stability of these negative temperature states. Theoretical analyses are supported by numerical simulations using both quantum Monte Carlo methods and Lanczos iterations. The results show that the condition of negative temperature can only be achieved at precise points, and in contrast, the Boltzmann distribution yields inaccurate outcomes due to its inability to account for discrete energy spectra. The stability of these negative temperature states is ensured by the oscillatory nature of the eigenstates, which precludes any possibility of decay. Theoretical and experimental studies have validated the existence of these negative temperature eigenstates in closed systems. The occurrence of these negative temperature eigenstates is attributed to the energy selectivity of the two-photon process, which two-photon cavity physics inherently possesses. The interaction with a dissipative cavity field results in the disappearance of these negative temperature states, indicating that negative temperatures can only be maintained in isolated systems. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Moreover, we demonstrate that the dark matter interaction should be strong enough to yield the correct relic abundance, and conclude that the dark matter self-scattering cross-section exceeds the minimal value required by cosmological observations.
